prayer.text: Saint Adalbert of Prague, pray for us.

cues.text: A Sick Child's Vow
Adalbert was born Vojtech around 956, probably at Libice in Bohemia, into the Slavnik family, one of the great noble houses of the land.
According to tradition, he fell gravely ill as an infant, and his parents vowed to give him to the Church if he recovered.
They kept the vow, sending him to study at Magdeburg under Archbishop Adalbert.
There the young Vojtech took his teacher's name at confirmation.
He returned to Bohemia, and in 982 the clergy and people of Prague chose him as their bishop.
He was invested at Verona and consecrated at Mainz on June 29, 983.
A Reformer Driven Out
Adalbert's episcopate collided almost at once with the habits of his people.
Sources of the time record his struggle against polygamy, married priests, markets held on Sunday, and the sale of Christian slaves to non-Christian buyers.
The resistance grew so strong that he left Prague and went to Rome around 988.
In Rome he lived as a monk, first at Monte Cassino and then at the monastery of Sts. Boniface and Alexius on the Aventine.
Pope John XV eventually sent him back to Prague, and he returned in 992.
He founded the Benedictine abbey of Brevnov, which the pope confirmed in 993.
Still, the old conflicts returned, and he left Bohemia a second time.
Missionary to Hungary and Poland
Rather than force himself on a diocese that would not receive him, Adalbert turned to peoples only beginning to hear the Gospel.
Tradition says he preached in Hungary at the court of Duke Geza, and that he baptized Geza's son.
Later historians dispute the details, but tradition identifies that son as the future St. Stephen of Hungary .
Adalbert then went to Poland, where Duke Boleslaw the Brave welcomed him.
Boleslaw became his friend and patron, and supported his plan to preach to the pagan Prussians on the Baltic coast.
Martyrdom on the Baltic Coast
In 997 Adalbert set out for Prussia with two companions.
Boleslaw supplied an armed escort and ships for the journey.
The Prussians were deeply hostile to the mission, and the party was attacked and killed on April 23, which was Good Friday that year.
The accounts differ on the details.
Some report that Adalbert was struck down with spears, and others that he was beheaded and his head set on a pole.
Every account agrees that he died a martyr's death at the hands of those he came to serve.
Legacy
Boleslaw ransomed the body of the martyr and had it brought to Gniezno.
Pope Sylvester II canonized Adalbert in 999, though one early chronicler places the canonization in the year 1000.
He is honored as patron of Poland, Bohemia, and Hungary.
On the thousandth anniversary of his death, Pope John Paul II spoke in Gniezno and called Adalbert "a great patron of our continent".
Adalbert's own career had been marked by two expulsions from his see and a mission that lasted only weeks.
Yet his witness bore fruit across Central Europe, and the Church remembers him as a pastor who gave his life for the faith.
